The biography of Yizong <note>original: 義宗</note>, named Bei, states he was the eldest son of Taizu. When the Huhar kingdom surrendered, Taizu renamed the nation East Dan and appointed Bei as the Human Sovereign King to govern it. When Taizhou ascended the throne, he designated Dongping as the Southern Capital and relocated Bei to reside there. Upon Bei's return to his domain, he ordered Wang Jiyuan to compose the Southern Capital Stele.

He composed the *Garden Poetry on Making Music* and the *Langyuan Collection*.

The *History of Liao* in the Biographies of the Imperial Clan concerning King Ping, Longxian, records that King Ping was intelligent and possessed vast learning. He was capable in poetry and his writings circulated widely in the world. 

He shot ten deer and captured nine of them.

The *History of Liao* in the Biographies of the Imperial Clan concerning Qian, named Jun, states he was the eldest son of Daozong. At age six, he was enfeoffed as the King of Liang. The following year, he accompanied the Emperor on a hunt. His arrows hit the target three times in succession. The Emperor looked to his attendants and said, "Since the time of my ancestors, our riding and archery have surpassed others. Though this child is young, he does not let that tradition fall." Later, encountering the Emperor's joy, a banquet was prepared.

Cutting a Paulownia leaf to make a jade scepter.

Liu Xiang's *Garden of Stories* <note>original: Shuo Yuan</note> records that King Cheng and Tang Shuyu were living in leisure. The King cut a leaf from a paulownia tree into the shape of a jade scepter and gave it to Tang Shuyu, saying, "I use this to enfeoff you." Tang Shuyu was delighted and informed the Duke of Zhou. The Duke of Zhou requested an audience and asked, "Did the Son of Heaven enfeoff Shuyu?" King Cheng replied, "I was only joking with Shuyu." The Duke of Zhou responded, "The Son of Heaven has no joking words." Consequently, Tang Shuyu was enfeoffed at Jin.

The Great Treasure and the Secret Books.

Ying Shao's *Comprehensive Meaning of Customs* <note>original: Fengsu Tong</note> records that An, the King of Huainan, recruited thousands of guests, practitioners of methods, and men of arts. He produced the *Great Treasure* and the *Secret Books* kept in a pillow within the garden.

The Eight Dukes arrived at the gate.

Ge Hong's *Biographies of Divine Immortals* records that Liu An, the King of Huainan, was the grandson of Emperor Gao of the Han. He was humble toward scholars and sincerely loved Confucian learning. Practitioners of methods traveled from a thousand miles away, drawn by his humble words and heavy gifts, to request an audience.

The gate official reported this to the King. The King sent the gatekeeper to intentionally challenge them with difficult questions. The Eight Elders all transformed into young children with hair tied in horn-shaped knots of raven-black silk and complexions like peach blossoms. The gate official was greatly alarmed. When the King heard of this, he did not even put on his shoes but went barefoot to welcome them. They ascended the Terrace for Contemplating Immortals. He spread brocade curtains and ivory beds, burned hundred-blend incense, and presented tables of gold and jade, observing the rituals due from a disciple to a teacher.

Chickens crow in the heavens; dogs bark amidst the clouds.
<term>Ge Hong</term> <gloss>283–343 AD, Taoist scholar and alchemist</gloss>, Traditions of Divine Immortals <note>original: "Shenxian Zhuan"</note>: Liu An, the King of Huainan, ascended the mountain to perform a great sacrifice and buried gold in the earth. He then ascended to heaven in broad daylight. The rocks on the mountain where the Eight Elders and Liu An stepped were all indented with their footprints. The people of that time passed down the story that when King Liu An was about to depart, he left the remaining medicinal vessels in the courtyard. The chickens and dogs licked and pecked at them, and all of them were able to ascend to heaven. Thus it is said: <term>chickens crow in the heavens and dogs bark amidst the clouds</term>.

Palace of Fish and Algae.
Ge Hong, Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital <note>original: "Xijing Zhaji"</note>: Liu Ruyi, the Prince of Zhao, was young and could not yet attend lessons with outside tutors. Lady Qi ordered the former tutor of the Prince of Zhao, Mother Zhao, to tutor him. Her chamber was named the Palace of Cultivating Virtue, which was later changed to the <term>Palace of Fish and Algae</term> <gloss>Yu Zao Gong</gloss>.

The Rock of the Falling Gibbon; The Cave of the Dwelling Dragon.
Ge Hong, Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital: King Xiao of Liang enjoyed the pleasures of constructing palaces, chambers, gardens, and enclosures. He built the Palace of Shining Splendor and constructed the Rabbit Garden. Within the garden was the Mountain of a Hundred Spirits. On the mountain were stones of diverse textures, the <term>Rock of the Falling Gibbon</term>, and the <term>Cave of the Dwelling Dragon</term>. There was also the Goose Pond, and within the pond were the Isle of Cranes and the Shore of Wild Ducks.

Visiting the Hall of Forgetting Cares
<margin>Ge Hong’s Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital: King Xiao of Liang <note>Liu Wu, a Han dynasty prince known for his patronage of the arts</note> visited the Hall of Forgetting Cares.</margin>
<margin>In the Hall of Forgetting Cares, he gathered various wandering scholars and asked each to compose a <term>fu</term> <gloss>rhapsodic poem</gloss>.</margin> Mei Cheng wrote the Poem on the Willow; Lu Qiaoru wrote the Poem on the Crane; Gongsun Gui wrote the Poem on the Patterned Deer; Zou Yang wrote the Poem on Wine; Gongsun Cheng wrote the Poem on the Moon; Yang Sheng wrote the Poem on the Screen. Han Anguo did not finish his Poem on the Table, so Zou Yang composed it on his behalf.

The flagon is filled with pale jade-colored wine; the goblet is offered with golden syrup.
<margin>Ge Hong’s Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital: Mei Cheng’s Poem on the Willow says:</margin>
The King’s temperament is deep and serene; he governs the elite and finds pleasure in them. I, your humble servant, though blind and deaf <note>a self-deprecating scholarly trope</note>, join in to offer these words. Thus, we have the wine that fills the pale jade flagon and the mash offered in the golden syrup. A thousand varieties of delicacies fill the six kitchens. # Dreams.

->By M.W. FRATER DR. W. WYNN WESTCOTT, IX°.<-
->Supreme Magus, Soc. Ros. in Ang.<-

DREAMS have at all times been a favourite subject for discussion, and the very little that is known about their causation has led to the utmost divergence in the opinions expressed concerning them.
All of us dream occasionally, and many persons dream as often as they sleep; probably we all do so, and the difference between persons as to dreaming is due to a variation in the power of Remembrance when awaking.
There is considerable evidence to show that animals dream as well as men, women, and children. Many of us must have observed the domestic cat and dog showing signs of dreaming by their movements and the sounds they make. Tennyson wrote—
> “ Like a dog he hunts in dreams—— ”
It has been said that animals in their wild state of nature do not dream, but it is difficult to make observations on wild animals. It is generally agreed that domestication is the cause of increased mind-power in some animals, and with enlarged powers of observation and concerted action, may come the faculty of dreaming. Domesticated animals certainly develop some Reason in addition to their primal Instinct, and this can only be due to the companionship of man and the training they receive; the mere change of food would not alone account for their extended powers.
To return to humanity, Byron wrote of dreams—
> “ Strange state of being . . . .
> Senseless to feel, and with sealed eyes to see ” ;
while Cato said—
> “ Regard not dreams, since they are but the images, of our hopes and fears.”
Wordsworth said that we may
> “ Hunt half a day for a forgotten dream.”
Joel, the old Hebrew prophet said—
> “ Your old men shall dream dreams,”
Dryden wrote—
> “ Dreams are interludes which fancy makes,”

# To the Most Serene and
## Most Mighty Sovereign and Lord/ Lord
### Gustav of Sweden/ King of the Goths and
### Wends &c./ my most Gracious
### Lord.

<meta>Large woodcut ornamental initial V featuring intricate floral and scrollwork designs, used to open the main body of the dedication text.</meta>

To describe the entire world as is my intention in this book, Most Mighty and Gracious Lord, requires a far-reaching and well-informed mind that has read much, seen much, heard much, and experienced much. Yet all this would still not be enough if a right judgment were not present, by which one might distinguish the true from the false, and the certain from the uncertain. After the books of Holy Scripture, there would be no reading on earth more pleasant and useful to man than the reading of histories, if they were written (as they should be) without regard for this or that party. For what are all histories other than illustrative examples in which one sees how this or that matter turned out? They show how human wisdom and foresight are so often uncertain, even blind, and how all things depend entirely on the hand of God, who works all things in all things. All our counsel goes backward where it is not in accordance with the providence of God. Look: the children of Adam wanted to build a tower reaching to heaven to escape the future flood. How far they failed is manifest to everyone. Ninus and Semiramis undertook to build invincible cities, namely Nineveh and Babylon. They made walls around them so wide that several wagons might go side by side. But it helped them nothing, as was found with time. The Romans wanted to claim for themselves an eternal reign and highest empire over the whole world. For that reason they also destroyed the African city of Carthage, which also undertook such a thing. But how long did they keep it? The Jews and after them the heathens wanted to root out Christ and his wholesome teaching against the counsel of God, but what did they accomplish? The Jews went to ruin because of it, and the heathens were taken from their error and false religion, however much they initially raged against it. The Holy Land formerly flowed with milk and honey, but now it is a smoky, bitter, and wild soil. Greece in those same times had the most ingenious and subtle men that could be found in the world, where also all philosophers and masters of nature arose. What does it have now but wretched, coarse, unlearned, and simple people? Sweden, Gothland, Norway and other northern lands were formerly so poor and needy in bodily sustenance that they could not raise their <term>indigenas</term> <gloss>natives</gloss> and countrymen. Instead, they sent them in large crowds into fertile lands. From there came the Goths, Lombards, Northmen, Cimbri, Swiss, Alemanni and many others. But in our times they surpass almost all lands of Europe in riches. Is there less found in them than in these outer lands? Where does one find more gold, silver, copper, and also other metals than in these lands? Where does one find handsomer cattle, and more meat and fish than in these lands? They give enough dried and salted fish to all of Germany, France, Bohemia and Poland. Everyone knows what precious skins and furs or lining-work come out of these lands into all southern countries. But where does it come from, that these lands which formerly could not nourish their inhabitants now feed them and send nourishment into other lands? It comes from the hand of God, who gives and

and takes away according to his pleasure. He shows with his deeds that he is the Lord, not only in heaven but also on earth and in the wide sea. All things are handled through him, and nothing <term>ex fortuna uel casu</term> <gloss>from fortune or chance</gloss>, as men speak of it, but everything happens out of the knowledge, indeed the order of God. From this it comes that one kingdom ends and another begins; one land becomes rich and another perishes; one city increases and another decreases; one lordship dies out and another rises. In summary, under the moving heavens nothing remains permanent; everything is subject to wonder. From this we should learn to set our hearts not on the perishable, but on the eternal. I write such things, however, not to teach Your Royal Majesty, who knows this well, but to give some indication of what caused me to describe this book. The argument extends very far. I wanted to dedicate here a compendium and short summary of all the lands of the earth to the common man, to delight himself therein with reading. I also wanted to show a way to the learned how one might yet write very useful Cosmographies and Topographies after so many German Chronographies. I undertook and began this work eighteen years ago, following that highly learned man Strabo. But while I was still occupied with this work six years ago, Your Royal Majesty's servant came to me, the highly learned Master Georgius Normannus. He was already familiar with me from several books published under my name. When he inspected this undertaken work, it seemed to him well worthy that it should come to light under the royal protection of Your Royal Majesty. Otherwise, I would not have been so bold as to present such a patron for this book. I also undertook this suggestion all the more gladly as I heard from him of the free and inclined spirit which Your Royal Majesty bears toward all the learned and skillful. This has been especially proven in that Your Majesty has been diligent to instruct the young princes, Your Royal Majesty's sons, in Christian virtues and noble arts. # Preface of Sebastian Münster
## to the Book of Cosmography
### or Description of the World.

<meta>Ornamental decorative initial D featuring interlaced foliate and vine patterns.</meta> All histories show us how highly and nobly the art called by a Greek word <term>Cosmographiam</term> <gloss>Cosmography</gloss>, that is, description of the world, or <term>Geographiam</term> <gloss>Geography</gloss>, description of the earth, has always been regarded by experienced men. Indeed, history is based on this art, and without it no one can describe a history in an orderly way or rightly understand it. As a wise and learned man says, <margin>What Geography is.</margin> Geography is a knowledge of the earth, which we mortals inhabit by the gift of God, which makes the lovers of art ready and prepared to understand the things that have happened, which have been left to us in writings from ancient times. Indeed, this art frequently opens to us the hidden secrets of Holy Scripture and reveals the power of clever nature that lies hidden in various things. How could the ancients, and also those who live in our time, have conducted wars so successfully in foreign and distant lands? They sometimes had to travel over high mountains, sometimes over deep waters, and also sail over seas. This would have been impossible if they had not known through the art the location of the earth, the width and end of the sea, and the properties of the lands. What do you think the kings in Spain suffered in costs and damages until they explored the lower part of the earth and discovered the navigation from Spain to the Orient through the south? In former times, people were considered highly intelligent and wise who had traveled far and been to many places, seen many cities, and experienced the manners and properties, customs and usages of people. They also learned and recognized many animals, trees <margin>In what regard Cosmography was held by the ancients.</margin> and the nature of herbs. Great honor was offered to them, and they were used as counselors for the common good and as judges of the people, as those who could give good and blessed advice through their own experience. For this art extends not only over the lands, dwellings and customs of various peoples, but also concerns itself with other things of the earth and sea, such as strange animals, trees, metals and other useful and useless things that are found on the earth or in the sea. In our times it is quite necessary that you wander far and wide on the earth to inspect and experience the location of lands, cities, waters, mountains and valleys. Likewise the manners, customs, laws, and government of people, and the properties and nature of animals, trees and herbs. You may now find these things in books and learn and recognize more from them about this or that land than another who has been there for a year and a day. Here you find how people in our times live so visibly and civilly among each other in communities, compared to the old and first times when people on earth lived poorly, simply, even boldly and crudely. They had no marked coins in use; there was no trade or merchant business, but they gave item for item and repaid one good deed with another. No one had anything special or private property, but just as the air and heaven were common, so also the earth and water were free to everyone.

First, to perform the preliminary retreat <term>nyenpa</term>: go to a secluded and pleasant place such as a charnel ground, and perform sweeping and so on to make the mind engaged. In that place, in front of yourself, make a mandala of one cubit. In its center, make a circle of one span. In its center, draw a single surplus-offering for the precious support. On top and outside of that, arrange heaps of grain. On the central heap, place a small table or a supreme footed-throne. On top of that, place a skull-cup <term>kapala</term> with the required marks, filled with the "glory-food" <term>palshö</term> and various kinds of blood, and arrange a single support <term>gtor ma</term>.

<leaf-break/>

...Offer many things that have been made, and make requests for the desired goals. Then, perform the preliminary retreat. As before, perform the generation and visualization at the four times of the day, and offer the <term>gtor ma</term>. Thus, practice for twenty-one days and keep it secret. Then, offer the support <term>gtor ma</term> in a clean place. Making the jewel and the body-form is the preliminary retreat. 
Then, for the accomplishment of the actual siddhi <term>spiritual attainment</term>: for the practice of this, on top of the previous altar, make a triangle one span in width and height. Coat its exterior and interior in red with blood and so on. In its three corners, plant three supreme ritual daggers <term>phur ba</term>. On top of it, place a skull-cup with the required marks, filled with various kinds of food. Also, pour various grains, grapes, and fruits inside it. Place various jewels there too. Inside it, place various kinds of food that you enjoy. On top of that, place the aforementioned jewel and the body-form. In the three corners and the front of the mandala, provide four <term>gtor ma</term> made of dough and beer, with small finger-pressed offerings...

Pour the first press of beer and place the two jewels inside it. Above that, seat the two figures of the Father and Mother <note>the deity and his consort</note>. Also, arrange a single regular offering <term>gtor ma</term> in front. Furthermore, arrange as many white and sweet offerings to the Triple Gem as you can afford. Establish a strict boundary and remain in a state of self-contained bliss. Possessing the <term>bodhicitta</term> <gloss>mind of enlightenment</gloss>, generate whichever <term>yidam</term> <gloss>meditational deity</gloss> of Chakrasamvara is appropriate and maintain the boundary strictly. Visualize the protective tent, the mountain of fire, the vajra-fence, and the celestial palace. Offer the <term>gtor ma</term> to the gurus, deities, and the Triple Gem. Pray that no obstacles arise to the accomplishment and that it be quickly achieved. Then, visualize that support offering as a mountain of flesh and blood and a great ocean of nectar. Upon it, instantly and vividly generate the two jewels and the support offerings as the Dharma Protector Father and Mother. Then, light rays radiate from the seed syllable in your own heart, inviting the Father and Mother from the charnel ground of Uddiyana in the west, and they dissolve into the visualization. Then, the flesh and blood of the offering <term>gtor ma</term>...

<leaf-break/>

...Place four containers, each filled with a bit of blood, among the other fourteen. Also, arrange whatever offerings for the Guru and Triple Gem and whatever feast substances <term>tsog</term> you have obtained. This explains the sequence of setting up the ritual materials and substances. Then, sitting comfortably and facing the west, enter the meditative absorption of the self-generated deity and establish the boundary by visualizing the protective wheel and tent. Offer the <term>gtor ma</term> to the gurus, deities, and Triple Gem according to the manual, and pray for protection from obstacles. Offer the first portion of the blessed feast food and the five <term>gtor ma</term>. Consume some yourself and send out the remaining offerings. Then, instantly bless the <term>gtor ma</term> with the syllables **OM AH HUM**. Visualize it as a great ocean of nectar and a great mountain of blood. Inside that, imagine a great palace of the charnel ground made of precious gems within a skull-cup. Inside that, from the white shell and the cowrie, the Dharma Protector Father and Mother are vividly generated. From the seed syllable in your own heart, light rays...
